title: The MD5 Message-Digest Algorithm
summary: Describes the MD5 message-digest algorithm, which takes input of any length and produces a 128-bit fingerprint, or message digest, of the input. It was meant for digital signature applications. It is informational, and MD5 is now known to be weak against deliberate collisions.

plainLanguage.summary: MD5 turns any file or message into a short 128-bit fingerprint. If the input changes even slightly, the fingerprint changes. It was meant to help check data integrity, but it is no longer considered safe against intentional collisions.

questions: how long is an md5 hash
subtitle: The 128-bit fingerprint algorithm that turns a message of any length into a short digest.

tldr.problem: Digital signature schemes need a way to shrink a large file into a small, fixed-size value that can be signed securely with a private key.
tldr.mechanism: MD5 pads the message, appends its length, then processes each 512-bit block through four rounds of 16 operations in a 128-bit buffer to produce a digest.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1321 is Informational (not a standard) and was updated by RFC 6151; the collision resistance it conjectured is no longer considered adequate.

today: RFC 1321 is Informational, not a standard, and it has been updated by RFC 6151, which describes known weaknesses in MD5.

sections.title: What MD5 Does
sections.content:
MD5 takes a message of arbitrary length and produces a 128-bit message digest. The RFC states as a conjecture that it is computationally infeasible to produce two messages with the same digest, or to produce any message with a given target digest. It is intended for digital signature applications, where a large file is compressed before being signed.

MD5 is designed to run efficiently on 32-bit machines and use little memory. It is assigned an OSI object identifier; in X.509 AlgorithmIdentifier, its parameters have type NULL.
sections.plainLanguage: MD5 squishes any message into a 128-bit code. If you change even one bit, the code should look completely different. It was designed to help verify a message hadn't been tampered with.

sections.title: Terminology and Notation
sections.content:
A word is a 32-bit quantity, and a byte is an 8-bit quantity. The algorithm specifies how sequences of bits map to bytes (high-order bit first) and to words (low-order byte first).

Operations are defined on words: addition modulo 2^32 (+), left circular shift (X <<< s), bitwise complement (not(X)), bitwise OR (X v Y), bitwise XOR (X xor Y) and bitwise AND (X Y, with XY meaning AND).
sections.plainLanguage: MD5 works on 32-bit chunks using simple bitwise operations. The notation is the standard math/bitwise notation used throughout the RFC.

sections.title: How MD5 Computes the Digest
sections.content:
To compute the digest of a b-bit message, MD5 does five steps:

  1. Padding: append bits so the length is congruent to 448 modulo 512. Padding is always added (a single 1 bit followed by enough 0 bits). Even if already aligned, padding is added.
  2. Append length: append a 64-bit representation of b (the original message length in bits), in little-endian word order. After padding and appending length, the message is a multiple of 512 bits.
  3. Initialize buffer: start with four 32-bit words: A = 0x67452301, B = 0xEFCDAB89, C = 0x98BADCFE, D = 0x10325476 (in little-endian order for the values).
  4. Process each 512-bit block: for each block, copy it into 16 32-bit words M[0..15] (little-endian). Save the current buffer (AA, BB, CC, DD). Then run four rounds, each with 16 operations, mixing M[i] with constants and the buffer words using nonlinear functions. The 64 constants are derived from the sine function. The result for the block is added to the saved buffer.
  5. Output: the final buffer A, B, C, D is the message digest, with A being the low-order 32 bits in the sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: MD5 first pads the message to a full 512-bit block with room for a length tag. It then runs each block through a mixer with four rounds of 16 steps, carrying over results. After processing all blocks, the four mixing registers form the final 128-bit fingerprint.

sections.title: Example and Notes on Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC gives an appendix with an example of computing MD5 for the string "abc", showing intermediate values. It notes that the digest is a sequence of 32 hexadecimal digits in the order A, B, C, D with low-order byte first within each word.

The document ends with test data for the example. It also includes a reference implementation in the appendix (informally described). The algorithm's security properties are stated as conjectures.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC includes an example and test values to help verify implementations. The output is just the four registers written out as bytes in order.

references.text: S. Turner, L. Chen, "Updated Security Considerations for the MD5 Message-Digest and the HMAC-MD5 Algorithms", RFC 6151, March 2011.
